newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: "Everyone a winner" from Papua New Guinea turmoil.
newsitem.headline: "Everyone a winner" from Papua New Guinea turmoil.

text.p: It was a crisis that could have blown up anywhere in the Third World, pitting military against elected government and police against protesters in a potentially explosive combination.
But only in the South Pacific could it have ended quite so suddenly, and quite so happily.
On Tuesday, Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan addressed parliament to defend his decision to hire foreign mercenaries to put down a long-running rebellion on Bougainville island.
An angry mob, including armed soldiers, gathered outside. Former colonial power Australia had its troops on standby ready to evacuate 10,000 of its nationals if the crisis escalated.

On Wednesday, Chan announced he was stepping aside for the good of the nation. Protesters outside parliament danced with joy and 10 days of tropical turmoil melted into an impromptu carnival on the streets of the capital.

"It was a win-win situation ... I think everyone in Papua New Guinea is a winner," smiled Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, the sacked army commander who started it all by demanding that Chan quit over the $36 million mercenary contract.
"There is a PNG way of doing things, there is a PNG style. And we have come out of it," the general added.
Analysts agreed with his assessment. It could have turned nasty, but there were no real losers from PNG's latest and deepest crisis.
The army wanted Chan to quit and the mercenaries out of the country. It got what it wanted, and kept millions of dollars of military hardware brought in by the mercenaries.
The rebels on Bougainville, 800 kms (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby, feared an assault by 70 well-armed African mercenaries. The assault never happened.

And Chan himself, with elections due in three months, was more concerned with saving face that hanging on to power. By defending the constitution against a military threat then standing aside for the good of the nation, he did just that.
The history of Papua New Guinea politics, where governments hardly ever last their course, shows Chan's turn is likely to come again.

The only loser, perhaps, was retired colonel Tim Spicer, who led the 70 mercenaries into the South Pacific only to find himself stuck in the British High Commission awaiting trial on illegal firearm charges.
But Spicer cannot complain too loudly -- his company walked away from the aborted assault millions of dollars richer without losing a man in action.
Dr Ron May, a Papua New Guinea specialist at the Australian National University, compared the PNG crisis to similar standoffs in Eastern Europe or the Middle East.
"I am personally surprised that it's all worked out as well as it has," May told Reuters on Thursday.

"If you're looking at images from Albania and Palestine and places, and considering how volatile you expect Papua New Guinea to be, the outcome of this whole thing has been remarkably, dare I say, civilised."
May said one crucial development was that parliament on Tuesday voted down an anti-Chan resolution even though cabinet ministers had begun to desert the prime minister.
"When it came to the crunch the compelling argument seems to have been that the parliament shouldn't stand down to a threat from the military," May said.

It is unclear, however, what effect the crisis will have on moves to resolve the crisis on Bougainville, where ragtag guerrillas operating on their own ground have successfully fought off the ill-equipped PNG army for nine years.
May said he was sure Chan's decision to bring in the Sandline mercenaries had set back the process of negotiation with the Bougainville Revolutionary Army "by some considerable amount of time".

He added: "What you have to do now is recover the lost ground, but with Chan standing aside for a while, with the possibility of a new government coming in, and with the peace package being negotiated, the process can get up and running."

If the conflict resumes, the rebels could find themselves up against a reinvigorated army. Former army commander Singirok said the crisis had brought the 4,600-strong defence force together as never before.
As to his own future, the general was less clear.
"I have not had leave since 1990. I will go home, fishing, thank you," a smiling Singirok told reporters.
